Search the Suttas and look words up in Dict.Dhamma.Gift — the dictionary by the Suttas and the Vinaya, with DPD, PTS, Gandhari, Sanskrit dictionaries and more beside it — on any website: select a word or phrase (or just click on a word) and the extension shows the dictionary entry right there, without leaving the page. In the extension's settings, pick where the result opens: Side Panel (the default; in Firefox the default is Popup, and Side Panel opens a window while the sidebar is closed), New Window, Popup, Dharmamitra (New Window), GoldenDict-NG, MDict (macOS) or a Custom URL (an https address). The default language is set there too (English or Русский). Right-click a selected phrase for either a Dhamma.gift text search or a full grammar breakdown via DharmaMitra. Right-click the extension's icon in the toolbar for quick links to Dhamma.gift, Dict.Dhamma.Gift, Aksharamukha and DharmaMitra. Toggle the extension on/off by clicking its icon or with Alt+Shift+X (Option+Shift+X on a Mac). To look up a selected word, press Alt+Shift+Z, or copy it twice quickly: Ctrl+C+C (⌘C C on a Mac); a checkbox in the settings turns the double copy off. In Firefox, Ctrl+Shift+Y (Cmd+Shift+Y on a Mac) opens the sidebar. Shortcuts can be changed in your browser's settings (Change shortcuts in the extension's settings leads there). Firefox Add-ons still has the earlier version 0.6.1. There Side Panel is the default, the toggle is Ctrl+Shift+X, the list also has Compact and DictTango App, and there is no Alt+Shift+Z or Ctrl+C+C. Opera has no listing of its own: install the extension from the Chrome Web Store (the Opera button above leads there). Tampermonkey script (also works on Safari: our Safari extension for macOS is not published yet): installation instructions. Only here are all six editions of the Pali Canon side by side: any text, line by line, with the differences highlighted, in one click. Tag Edition Country, original script Type of edition Source SR Siam Rath 1927 Thailand, Thai national E-Tipitaka BJT Buddha Jayanti (1957-1993) Sri Lanka, Sinhala national Tipitaka.lk VRI Chaṭṭha Saṅgāyana (Sixth Council, 1954-1956) Myanmar, Burmese national Tipitaka.org MS05 Mahāsaṅgīti 2005, as printed Roman script derived: the Sixth Council edition (Myanmar) in Roman script Tipitaka2500 MS Mahāsaṅgīti Roman script derived from MS05: SuttaCentral's segments and edits SuttaCentral PTS Pali Text Society (from the 1880s) UK, Roman script critical, European: from manuscripts of Sri Lanka, Myanmar and Thailand GRETIL A tag leads to the edition's known problems, below. Column order: the national editions first, from fewer late texts in the Khuddaka Nikāya to more: SR, BJT, VRI. Then the Mahāsaṅgīti, the printed one (MS05) first, then SuttaCentral's version (MS), and PTS last, a critical edition. Columns you arrange yourself keep your order. There are three national editions: SR, BJT, VRI. MS05 and MS are derived from the Myanmar one, which is why they are almost the same as VRI. In the late Khuddaka Nikāya books Siam Rath has none of the Milindapañha, Nettippakaraṇa and Peṭakopadesa, Buddha Jayanti has the last two, Chaṭṭha Saṅgāyana all three.

✦ → Compare on any line opens the text with every edition and every translation in your languages, differences on; your own Compare settings stay as they were. The Compare reader mode (Alt+Shift+2) shows by default every edition, a translation in your main language and the differences. What you change there (editions, lines or columns, translators, differences) is kept. Choose the editions in Settings or the reader's quick settings. In columns (Alt+C), a column's name (▾) opens a menu to put another edition or a translation in it, and − / + remove or add a column. The Differences switch highlights where an edition departs from the reading of the national editions shown (SR, BJT, VRI): their majority decides. MS05, MS and PTS are marked where they differ from it but do not vote. With one national edition shown, it is the reference; with none, every edition shown votes. Try it: sn56.11.

The Dhamma.Gift app for iPhone, iPad and Android: search and read the Pāli Canon — Suttas and Vinaya in Pāli with Russian and English translations — with or without an internet connection. Free, no ads, no tracking, no account needed.

Download the library once and everything works in airplane mode: search, the table of contents, the texts with their translations, and the dictionary. You choose what goes on the device: Settings → Offline library → Choose…. The Mahāsaṅgīti is required (it holds the contents and search); the other Pali editions and the translation languages are up to you, and the texts you leave out open online. Voices can be downloaded too, so reading aloud also works offline (Voice). The download keeps going in the background and with the screen locked. Until then the app works online, exactly like the site. When the library has new files, the Offline library update bar offers Update. Change… in the same row changes the choice or deletes the library (Remove all) any time.

Full-text search over the whole canon, right on the device: infix matches (kacchapa finds mahākacchapānaṁ), diacritics optional, filters by collection and translator, and a match context that opens straight in the reader (Search). In the reader: a text beside its translation, reading modes, Pāli in other scripts. Tap a Pāli word — the dictionary opens, offline too. Tap a paragraph — it is read aloud (Voice). The app opens where you left off: the last search, a text, the contents or Memo (Settings → On start, open).

Share to Dhamma.Gift. Select a word or a passage in any other app or site → Share → Dhamma.Gift, and the search results open right away. On iPhone they appear in the share sheet itself, without leaving the app you were in. A shared dhamma.gift link opens that text. Shortcuts on the icon. A long press on the app icon. On Android: favorites & history, plus either your 3 most recent texts or Contents, Memo and Dictionary (Settings → Recent texts in app shortcuts). On iPhone: favorites & history and your 3 most recent texts; Siri and the Shortcuts app can open Dhamma.Gift, a section (Contents, Memo, Dictionary…) or a search. In the text-selection menu. Select text in any app, and Dhamma.Gift in the selection menu opens the search. Android. The phone's own search. In Android's system search Dhamma.Gift is offered as a place to search: the query opens as a search in the app. The texts you read recently show up there too. Android. Quick Settings and Control Center. A Dhamma.Gift button in the notification shade on Android and in Control Center on iPhone: one tap from anywhere, offline. Player on the lock screen. While a text is read aloud or a recording plays (the Pātimokkha's sections), its player is in the notification shade and on the lock screen. Android. Links open in the app. A dhamma.gift link tapped in a messenger or in notes (https://dhamma.gift/mn1) opens the text in the app, not in the browser. Reminders on schedule. Subscriptions — a text or a word to come back to — can remind you at a set time with a notification; a browser can't promise that with the tab closed.

Fixes reach the app from the site, without a store update: when new files have come in, the New version available bar offers Update (the page reloads) or Later. Settings → App version shows the version; its check button looks for an update, says the result in a word or two (Up to date, Update available, Offline…) and then offers the next step: Update, Retry, or Store when the update needs a newer version of the app.
Favorites, history, notes and settings stay on the device. Signing in is optional and only syncs them between your devices (Login).

Windows 10 and 11: Dhamma.Gift in the Microsoft Store — the site in its own window, always the current version. PWA: the site installed from the browser, with an icon, shortcuts and the same offline library (not in a private window).

Dict.Dhamma.Gift is a dictionary by the Suttas and the Vinaya: a word means what the Suttas and the Vinaya themselves say it means — in their definitions and in their similes. Definitions from the Suttas and the Vinaya. For 800 key terms of the glossary — 702 of them defined in the Suttas and the Vinaya — it gives the Pali definition, word for word, and every line in the Suttas and the Vinaya where it stands (Katamañca, bhikkhave, dukkhaṁ? … — DN 22, MN 9, MN 141 and six more for dukkha), with the Dhamma.Gift rendering in English and Russian. Special definitions, given for one context (ariyassa vinaye), are marked. Where the Suttas call something else by the word (adhivacana), that is shown too: dukkha → kāma desire, from ‘dukkhan’ti, bhikkhave, kāmānametaṁ adhivacanaṁ (AN 6.23:1.2, AN 8.56:1.2). Inflected forms find the term too: dukkhassa, dukkhena, dukkhato. Then, in the order the word page shows them: DPD (Digital Pāḷi Dictionary); Sutta-Vinaya Definitions and Similes — for any word, the places where the Suttas and the Vinaya define it and the similes that explain it; the Gandhari Dictionary (M. Cone and others); PTS; Buddhadust; Wisdom Library; and 30+ Sanskrit dictionaries — one search, every source on one page. It is a separate site, dict.dhamma.gift, and an app; it is also built into Dhamma.Gift: it pops up when you click a Pali word while reading, and it opens in the "Dict" tab of the Quick Window.

documents.t: The dictionary is connected right here: click a Pali word — bhagavā, dukkha, nibbāna. The icon turns the dictionary on and off; on the site Alt+A does the same.

Below is a real reader page with Quick Settings open. In the "Dictionary" block pick the language and the mode, then click any Pali word in the text. On the site Quick Settings open from the sliders icon in the search field or with Alt+S. Open in a new window Modes in the list: the built-in DPD, Dict.DG in a popup, in a new window or mini, DharmaMitra.org, search only, and external apps (DPD Android, DictTango Android, Mdict iOS, GoldenDict-NG Desktop). Alt+B switches the mode. For a key term of the project's glossary, the popup's first line, marked (DG), gives the Dhamma.Gift rendering and, after def., every sutta where the Suttas or the Vinaya define the word; a special definition (one they give for a particular context) shows that Pali phrase in italics instead of def. A second line, adhivacana →, names what the Suttas call by this word, with those suttas. The built-in DPD mode works fully offline: the definitions from the Suttas and the Vinaya and DPD's short meanings load once (as a script, in English or Russian) and every lookup after that runs locally in the browser — no request to dict.dhamma.gift or anywhere else. It is meant for reading with no or a poor connection; the full Dict.Dhamma.Gift below has every source. If a word isn't in the built-in DPD, the popup offers two links instead: Search on Dhamma.gift and Search in the full Dict.Dhamma.Gift.

documents.t: A click opens one word. To look up a phrase or translate a whole sentence, turn on multi-select — the selection icon in the reader toolbar or Alt+J — and select that part of the Pali text. After 3 seconds the selection opens by itself in the dictionary of the chosen mode. For translating and parsing a sentence, the DharmaMitra.org mode or a right click on the Dict.Dhamma.Gift button in the dictionary window works best. The delay (3 or 5 seconds) can be changed in Settings, under "Multi-select".

Button What it does 🔍 Searches the texts on Dhamma.Gift for the word Dict.Dhamma.Gift logo (middle button) Opens the word in the full dictionary — dict.dhamma.gift The same button with a right click, a middle click or a long tap on a phone Opens DharmaMitra — grammar analysis of the word ✕ Closes the window (Esc) Drag the window by its title and resize it from the bottom right corner.

Dict.Dhamma.Gift: the definitions from the Suttas and the Vinaya and the Dhamma.Gift rendering first, then DPD, Sutta-Vinaya Definitions and Similes, the Gandhari and PTS dictionaries, Buddhadust, Wisdom Library and Sanskrit dictionaries, in one place. Open in a new window The same dictionary is on the site at dhamma.gift/dict, and it works offline there. Add a word to the address to open its page: dhamma.gift/dict/dukkha.

On the left — favorite and recent words. The clock button in the header hides and shows this column; on a phone it opens the list. Next to the word — ☆ to favorites (Alt+Q), 🔊 read aloud (Alt+R), copy the word and a link to it. Under the word — how many texts and matches Dhamma.Gift search finds for it, and "Open on Dhamma.Gift", which runs that search (Alt+3 does the same). For a key term of the glossary, the Dhamma.Gift rendering and Defined in: — every sutta where the word is defined; where the Suttas call something else by the word, an adhivacana → line with those suttas. Double-clicking any word inside an entry also searches for it. The dictionary blocks can be moved up and down (↑/↓). In the Sanskrit block, +/− expands or collapses all its dictionaries.

The menu (Alt+M) is one panel: Find on the page (Alt+F) — search the open entry, the same as on the site. Appearance — interface language, dark, light or auto theme, font size (Alt+− / Alt+= / Alt+0), sans or serif font, niggahita spelling (ṃ/ṁ). Expand right away — which entry sections open at once (grammar, examples, summary) and the "one section at a time" mode. Text and sound — the sandhi mark (’), the read-aloud voice, project links. Data — the offline dictionary, clearing history and favorites, resetting settings. Help (?, Alt+H) and Share are icons in the menu header. On dhamma.gift/dict the menu also has Compass (Alt+P) — the Dhamma.Gift quick window with the site's favorites and history, key suttas and Memo.

Under Menu → Data, a download button saves the dictionary right in the browser (~3.9 MB; on the Russian page ~6.1 MB, with the English meanings too): definitions by the Suttas: for a key term, links to the suttas where the Suttas themselves define the word, with the project's rendering; DPD's short meanings. The page itself is saved too, so it opens with no network. Once downloaded, it works as an automatic fallback: if a live lookup can't reach the server, this page shows short entries from the downloaded data instead — no separate "offline mode" to turn on, it just kicks in when needed. The button turns into delete once the data is downloaded, to free the space back up.

The book button in the search box (or Alt+S) opens the same word in other dictionaries and resources: Dhamma.Gift and DharmaMitra.org — search the texts and grammar analysis. Pali dictionaries — PTS Dictionary, Cone (Gandhari.org), DPR Analysis, Critical Pali Dictionary (CPD). Sanskrit dictionaries — Monier-Williams and other dictionaries from sanskrit-lexicon.uni-koeln.de, Glosbe Pāḷi-Sanskrit, Sanskrit Dictionary, LearnSanskrit. Other resources — WisdomLib, Google Custom Search, Aksharamukha (script converter).

The app for phones has a few things of its own: Select a word in any app (Android) — Dict.Dhamma.Gift appears in the text-selection menu next to Copy (or under ⋮) and opens the word. Share — share a word or a link to Dict.Dhamma.Gift. On iPhone and iPad the entry opens right in the share sheet. Pāḷi letters above the keyboard — ā ī ū ṁ ṅ ñ ṭ ḍ ṇ ḷ and a Paste key; "…" adds a second row for Sanskrit. The row can be turned off in the menu. Recent words on the icon (Android) — long-press the app icon to open one of your last words. Quick open (Android) — a Quick Settings tile.

Dict.Dhamma.Gift is a separate site you can open directly: dict.dhamma.gift. It also works outside Dhamma.Gift as a browser extension (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Opera), in the side panel by default (in Firefox, a popup). The DPD popup dictionary is available as a Tampermonkey script (installation); the plugin can be embedded on any site (details).

documents.t: Terms rendered according to the Principles by Suttas, with definitions from the Suttas and the Vinaya where they exist. The Pali definition is quoted verbatim, with links to the reader. The Dhamma.gift ecosystem is several independent git repositories that together make up one product: Repository What it is dg-node The main site (Fastify): search, reader, the site's API and the MCP server dg-docs This docs portal (Docusaurus, EN and RU) dg-apps The apps: Dhamma.Gift, Uposatha and the Dictionary (Capacitor, Android and iOS). The DG app builds its UI from a dg-node checkout, nothing is copied by hand pali-tts The voice service behind api.dhamma.gift/api/tts, and the Pāḷi pronunciation rules dg The legacy PHP site — the source of assets (assets/), 4nt, the TTS player (read/) and old pages (config/, login/, memo/) that dg-node links to via symlinks offline-data The project's own translations (best ru/en translation, second opinion, AI translation) suttacentral/sc-data The external SuttaCentral repository — Pali texts and translations in Bilara format (not ours, public) dgift_bot The Telegram bot (Python) dictPlugin The browser extension (Chrome/Firefox/Safari) + userscript Only the site itself (dg-node) can be brought up fully automatically with one script — everything else (the legacy repo, the texts) it uses as external data, wired in via symlinks (see CLAUDE.md → "Prod: paths and symlinks"), not as npm dependencies.

Requires Node.js 22.5 or newer, npm and git. The version floor is not a preference: the server reads its search database through node:sqlite, which only exists from 22.5 on. setup.sh checks this first and stops with a clear message rather than letting it fail later. git clone https://github.com/dhammagift/dg-node.git cd dg-node ./scripts/setup.sh # a few minutes, mostly cloning the texts ./scripts/start.sh # → http://localhost:3000 That is the whole thing. setup.sh does, in one pass: Sparse-clones three external repositories next to dg-node — by default into ../dg-data/: suttacentral/sc-data (sc_bilara_data/, structure/) — Pali texts dhammagift/offline-data (dhammagift/) — the project's translations dhammagift/dg (assets/, 4nt/, config/, login/, memo/, read/) — legacy assets Rebuilds the symlinks siteroot/{assets,4nt,config,login,memo,read} and siteroot/data/{suttacentral.net,dhammagift} so they point at the fresh clones (the same thing CI does, just without sudo or system paths — this version is meant for a regular dev machine). npm install in the dg-node root. Clones the built docs portal (the dist branch of dg-docs) into dg-docs/, so /docs works right away. npm run build-search-db — dg.db, the SQLite/FTS5 corpus the production server reads. Around 900 MB and a minute or two; this is the slow step. node test-search-db.js — asserts the freshly built database is sane before you ever start the server. Safe to re-run: already-cloned repositories are left alone (unless --force is passed), symlinks are just rebuilt, the databases are rebuilt from scratch. DATA_DIR=/other/path ./scripts/setup.sh — if you'd rather not clone next to dg-node. Check it works: http://localhost:3000/search?q=kacchapa&scope=dhamma&langs=ru,en http://localhost:3000/dn22:1.1

The docs portal (what you're reading now) is its own repository, dg-docs, built in two locales: git clone https://github.com/dhammagift/dg-docs.git && cd dg-docs npm install npm run build # English version → build/ npm run build:ru # Russian version → build-ru/ dg-node/dg-docs/ is a git-ignored clone of that repository's dist branch (the built pages, which CI publishes); setup.sh clones it, and the servers refresh it from dist (a test host may follow dist-preview).

The Fastify server exists because grep was not the slow part: a full-corpus /search?q=dukkha took about 42 seconds, of which raw grep was half a second — the rest was re-reading thousands of JSON files to fill in quotes, translations and titles for the hits. Moving the whole corpus into SQLite made that enrichment an indexed lookup instead of a filesystem walk, and the same query now answers in roughly two seconds.

documents.t: npm run build-search-db # → dg.db, about 900 MB, ~85 seconds The build reads the corpus directly — the same trees scripts/setup.sh wires up — and derives everything it needs itself. dg.db is generated and git-ignored. Never hand-edit it: the next build replaces the file wholesale. Anything written by a person — translator credits, reader modes, translator priority — lives in configs/ instead. To check a freshly built database: node test-search-db.js It asserts the invariants a silent build regression would break: that the corpus is actually there, that the index does substring matching rather than prefix matching, that diacritics and ё/е fold, that hidden translations stay out of the index, that no segment is stored twice, and that the search queries use indexes instead of scanning.

The server reads the database through node:sqlite, built into Node since 22.5 — there is no better-sqlite3 or other native module to compile. That also makes the Node version a hard requirement rather than a preference: on anything older, require('node:sqlite') throws ERR_UNKNOWN_BUILTIN_MODULE and the server does not start.
npm run start:fastify # port 3000 PORT=3005 npm run start:fastify # or anywhere else

pm2 start dg-fastify.js --name dg-fastify -i 2 --max-memory-restart 700M pm2 save Two things are worth knowing before doing that. PM2 spawns cluster workers with its own Node, not the one on your PATH. If the PM2 daemon was started under an older Node, every worker dies the instant it reaches require('node:sqlite') — and because PM2 pipes a cluster worker's output through IPC, it dies before anything reaches the log, so you get an endless restart loop with empty log files. Fork mode hides the problem, since it launches a fresh node from PATH. Check with ls -l /proc/$(pgrep -f 'God Daemon')/exe; fix by pointing the PATH in /etc/systemd/system/pm2-root.service at a current Node, then systemctl daemon-reload && pm2 save && pm2 update. Set a memory ceiling. Each worker holds its own copy of the transliteration runtime and settles around 550–600 MB under load, so two workers on a 4 GB machine is comfortable and three is not. max_memory_restart restarts a worker that grows past the limit while the other keeps serving. Clustering is worth it because a heavy search occupies the event loop for its whole duration — node:sqlite is synchronous and the enrichment is CPU-bound JavaScript. On a single process a cheap query issued during a heavy one waits for it (measured: 0.07 s alone, 2.2 s behind a dukkha search); with two workers it is answered immediately.

Requires: Python 3.9+. git clone https://github.com/dhammagift/dgift_bot.git cd dgift_bot ./setup.sh The script creates a venv (telegram/), installs the dependencies (python-telegram-bot>=20, watchdog) and drafts two config files — config.dgift_bot.json and config.dhammagift_bot.json (it's the same code, two bot accounts under different names — see the Telegram bot page). Fill in a real TOKEN in each. Then: telegram/bin/python main.py config.dgift_bot.json For a production setup (systemd services, autostart for both bots) — install_sysctl_bots.sh in the same repository. The short meanings in the bot's answers come from the dictionary files of dg-node (public/overrides/js/standalone-dpd/). dpdmini.py converts them once into dpd_mini.sqlite next to the bot (about 30 MB, not in git, built at the first query) and checks once a month whether the files are newer, rebuilding in the background. The path to dg-node is set at the top of dpdmini.py. Word autocomplete and watcher.py's notifications expect a dg-node running alongside (they read assets/texts/...) — the bot doesn't crash without it, those features just silently stay off.

Dhamma.gift is a set of connected tools built around the Pali Canon (Sutta and Vinaya) and its translations: search, a line-by-line reader, a Pali dictionary, and a text-to-speech player, tied together so that finding a passage, reading it with a translation, listening to it, and memorizing it are all one continuous workflow rather than separate apps. Any text can also be read in six Pali editions of the Canon at once, with the differences highlighted.

Six editions of the Canon, the differences in one click. A set of tools for voicing canonical texts, built right into the reading flow instead of living in a separate playback app. 1. Dhamma.Gift doesn't need an account or an email address. "Login" here means cloud sync of your favorites, history, subscriptions, reading progress and settings across devices — three ways to do it: Google — a regular Google account sign-in. Apple — Sign in with Apple, with your Apple ID. Apple may let you hide your e-mail; we then only get a private relay address from Apple. Secret Passphrase — fully anonymous: type a phrase of at least 8 characters and press Anonymous Login (no email, no password). Anyone who types the same phrase on another device gets access to the same synced data — treat it like a password. Open in a new window

Logging in (any of the three ways) on a device that already has its own history or favorites shows a choice: Merge Data — keep what's already on this device and add the cloud data on top of it. Overwrite from Cloud — wipe this device's data and pull down the cloud copy instead.
documents.s: If the device already has local data

documents.t: Sync — force a sync right away instead of waiting for the automatic one. Active devices — a list of every device currently signed in with this same phrase/account, with its device model and browser (detected automatically, nothing you type in) and last-active time. Three different actions are easy to mix up — they don't touch the same data: Action Where you click it What it wipes Logout On this device Nothing — it just turns off sync on this device. Local and cloud data are both left alone. Delete account & cloud data On this device Everything in the cloud (history, favorites, subscriptions, progress, settings, the account itself). Doesn't touch local data on this device. All sessions are deleted too, so every other signed-in device wipes its local data. With Google or Apple you sign in again to confirm. Terminate session (the ⏻ icon next to another device in the list) Remotely, from any device in the list Disconnects THAT device from the cloud and wipes all of its local data (except language and theme) — the confirmation prompt warns you about this honestly. "Terminate session" is not just a remote sign-out Clicking ⏻ on your OWN second device (say, your phone, thinking "I'll just close that extra session") wipes everything on that phone the next time it touches the network: history, favorites, reading progress, settings. Only use it on devices that are genuinely lost or shouldn't have access anymore.

On the site, the login page also has Backup and Restore. Backup saves this device's favorites, settings and recent history (the newest 84 entries) to a JSON file. Restore loads such a file back; records from the file replace matching data on this device. It all happens in the browser, and no account is needed. The apps don't show these buttons.

The phrase is normalized (lowercased, spaces → hyphens) and hashed on your device (SHA-256) before anything is sent to the cloud — the hash, not the phrase itself, is what identifies your data in the cloud.

documents.t: The "Memorize & Meditate" tool — build a custom audio session from any text: precise slicing by period/comma/line, custom repetition counts and pause durations, an end-of-cycle gong, MP3 export, a standalone interval-timer mode, and a first-letter visual-cue mode for memorization. You don't have to paste text in by hand to get here either — "Memorize" in the reader's context menu opens Memo already filled in with the passage you clicked. Open in a new window

The "Transform" button turns pasted text into a row of first letters, one per word — the classic memorization technique where you hold the whole text in your head and the page only shows you the anchor letters. Clicking a letter doesn't just reveal the full word in a tooltip — it also opens that word's dictionary entry right next to it: For a whole canonical text, switch reader modes instead of copying "Transform" is for your own text — notes, a hand-picked set of lines. To read an entire sutta this way, don't copy it in here — switch the reader to "For Memorization" mode instead (Alt+Shift+3, see Reading modes) — same first-letter trick, applied directly to the live sutta text, with its translation, and no manual copying.

If a text goes the other way and uses shorthand like "…pe…" or "etc." (peyyāla, the standard convention in Pali texts for not spelling out a repetitive list in full), the ✨ AI Expand button sends the text to ChatGPT with a ready-made prompt: recognize the pattern (the five aggregates, the six sense bases, the twelve links of dependent origination, the 32 parts of the body, and so on) and expand the shorthand into the full text in the original language. AI Expand opens an external ChatGPT tab The text is passed to chatgpt.com in the address bar, like any ordinary link with a parameter. Nothing is saved on Dhamma.gift and nothing passes through the app's own server.

The list icon opens a set of ready-made sessions — not just to try out the tool, but usable as standalone practice material: Ānāpānasati (mindfulness of breathing, the AN/MN formula), Sampajānapabba, a breakdown of the five aggregates (khandha), a passage on Dukkhasamudayaṁ Ariyasaccaṁ, Ādittasutta (SN 35.28, "All Is Burning"), and a list of idle-talk topics (tiracchānakathā) — each already set up with its own separator, pauses and repeat count.

The Selfcheck links (see Links below) open a quiz on the bhikkhu or bhikkhunī Pātimokkha. It shows one random rule. You can hide the rule's class and name to test yourself. Next shows another rule, and Rule Sets lets you choose which classes of rules to include.

Split by — how to cut the text into pieces (period, comma, line, etc.). Interval (sec) — the pause between pieces. End Wait (sec) — a separate, usually longer pause at the end of the whole cycle. End Sound — the sound at the end of the cycle: Tick, Gong or None. Loop — how many times to repeat (∞ by default). Translation — read the translation instead of / alongside Pali. Auto-cursor — when playback stops, puts the cursor at the end of the current line. The trash icon in the panel's corner (Reset settings) brings these back to the defaults and puts back the default text; it asks first. A finished session can be downloaded as an MP3 (Download MP3, the download icon) — say, to listen offline or outside the browser. Save (the disk icon) puts the session — its text and settings — into your favorites, and Share link copies a link that opens Memo with the same text and settings (up to 1,900 characters of text).

When you download a session as an MP3: DG voice — the interval and the end wait can each be up to 1 hour; the whole file up to 3 hours; the speech itself up to 30 minutes (pauses do not count towards it). Up to 200 lines and 20,000 characters of text. Google voice — pauses up to 10 seconds. See also Voice / TTS for the simpler player built right into the reader, without slicing or repeats.

The buttons are yours to rearrange MultiTool supports customization: reordering buttons, adding your own with your own icons, hiding the ones you don't need. Details in Make it your own below. MultiTool is the set of links on the Dhamma.gift home screen — a Dhamma multi-tool gathering links to key Pali and Dhamma resources, study materials, and utilities: Read Pāḷi, External (other Pali editions), Subscriptions, AI & Dicts, Materials, Tools, Favorites, history, subscriptions and Help. Some of what the tiles hold: External — S.4nt.org (also at s.dhamma.gift) shows the Thai, BJT and CST editions of the Pali text side by side. Subscriptions — a text a day, with reminders. Opens the Subscriptions tab of the Quick Window. AI & Dicts — Google Custom Search (/cse) runs your query over a set of Dhamma sites. Materials — Hatthipada (how the suttas define every word of the four noble truths), Declensions (a declension trainer) and Patimokkha (a Patimokkha trainer). Tools — the Uposatha days calendar by the Suttas, Old.Dhamma.Gift (the previous version of the site), Sutta Difference (compare two suttas), List Difference, Line to List, Blurbs (build a JSON of sutta summaries), and the Loop Timer, Repeat timer #2 and Pomodoro timers. Know a site or app that belongs here? Tell us via Contacts. Open in a new window

The set of tiles isn't fixed — open the burger menu (☰), all the way at the bottom, under "Settings": Add your own button — your own link with fields for Label (up to 24 characters), Address (you can drop {{q}} into it — it gets replaced with whatever's currently in the search box), Description (optional, a line under the button label), and an Icon — pick one from the built-in set or type your own emoji: Edit buttons — a list of every tile (built-in and your own) with a visibility checkbox next to each: uncheck it and the tile disappears from the home screen, check it again and it comes back. Clicking a tile in this list opens it for editing — you can change the label, address, description and icon even on a built-in tile (after that it stops auto-updating along with the rest of the site; "Restore original" in the button's edit form undoes the edit and turns auto-updating back on): Tile order — on the home screen itself, tiles can be dragged: with a mouse, just drag (a small initial movement starts the drag, so it doesn't interfere with a plain click); on a phone, press and hold for roughly a quarter-second, then drag (so it doesn't interfere with scrolling). The new order saves the moment you let go. Reset buttons — this option only shows up in the "Settings" menu when there's something to reset (something hidden, the order changed, or buttons of your own added). It brings back the original set and order of tiles; if you've added tiles of your own, those get deleted for good in the process (DG warns you and asks for confirmation first — there's no way to bring them back afterward). Your own buttons, edits, custom emoji icons and the tile order are NOT synced to the Cloud — they stay purely local to this particular browser.

Each tile like "External", "AI & Dicts" or "Materials" opens a list of links on that topic. Some of them already carry a gold star — the project's own editorial pick. A long-press (on phones) or right-click (on desktop) on the icon to the left of a link in that list toggles a star for you personally, on top of the editorial one — say, to remove a star from something you don't care for, or mark your own favorite resource. These personal marks are also stored only in this browser, not in the Cloud.

An episode is one sutta or a group of short suttas (a vagga). Its description links to that text on Dhamma.Gift, in Pali with the translations side by side. We are committed to the principle of maximum user anonymity. The Dhamma.gift project is designed to ensure that searching for and reading Pali texts does not require users to reveal their personal identity.

Telegram Services Telegram Bots: @Dhammagift_bot (main bot for sutta search and Pali dictionary lookups), @Dgift_bot (shortname alias). Telegram Mini Apps: Search, Reader, Dictionary. Apps (each one: PWA, Android, iOS and Windows) Dhamma.Gift — PWA · Android · iOS · Windows Dict.Dhamma.Gift — PWA · Android · iOS · Windows Uposatha (Uposatha calendar; "Uposatha by the Suttas" on the App Store and Microsoft Store) — PWA · Android · iOS · Windows The apps work online and offline. Throughout this policy an iOS app behaves exactly as the Android one does. Browser Extensions Chrome Extension Firefox Add-on Microsoft Edge Add-on Safari Extension for macOS (App Store: "Dict.Dhamma.Gift Extension", not published yet). The app that installs it only opens Safari's settings; it collects nothing.

This is an opt-in feature available on the website and within the PWA and the Android and iOS applications, used solely to synchronize your history, favorites, reading progress, subscriptions, and settings across multiple devices. Infrastructure — data is stored in Google Firebase (a third-party cloud database). Authentication methods: Anonymous passphrase — if you use a secret passphrase, it is hashed locally on your device (SHA-256) before transmission. Only the anonymous identifier is stored; your original passphrase never reaches the database. Google Account — we use your email address solely for session identification. Firebase Authentication (Google) keeps the email as your provider gives it, so you can see which account you are signed in with. Sign in with Apple — as with Google: we receive your Apple user identifier and the email address Apple provides (if you choose "Hide My Email", this is a private relay address created by Apple) and use them solely for session identification. Data storage — only your bookmarks (favorites, including quotes saved for memorization in Meditate & Memorize), search history, reading progress in texts, Daily Reading subscriptions with their read marks, and your settings (including the text on the Memo page) are saved. This data is accessible only to you upon successful authentication. Data deletion — you may permanently delete all your cloud data at any time using the "Delete account & cloud data" button in the Sync menu.

Our products process only the minimal technical data required for core functionality: Search — only search queries, text references, or selected dictionary terms are transmitted. Like every request, they appear in the web server's access logs with your IP address for 14 days. Synchronization — when enabled, we keep a list of your signed-in devices (device model, OS, browser and the full user agent) to help you manage them. Uposatha calendar (Uposatha app) — the place you share (rounded to about a kilometre) and your settings stay on your device; the sun and moon times are calculated on the device, and reminders are set on the device itself. The downloaded .ics file is also made on your device. Two things do reach dhamma.gift: the calendar page asks for its app manifest with your time zone and interface language in the address; if you subscribe to the calendar (Apple Calendar, Google Calendar or a copied link), the feed address contains your place rounded to about 1 km, your time zone and your reminder settings. Your calendar app fetches this address from dhamma.gift; if you subscribe in Google Calendar, Google's servers fetch it and Google sees the address too. We do not store these: the feed is computed on request and kept in memory for at most an hour, and the address appears only in the standard server logs (see Logs below). Browser extensions (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari) — the extension runs on the pages you visit so that it can look up a word you click or select; it does not read, store or send anything else from those pages. A word is sent only when you look it up: by default to dict.dhamma.gift (the "Search" button sends it to dhamma.gift). If you choose another destination, the word goes there instead: dharmamitra.org (the DharmaMitra mode and the "Explain grammar (DharmaMitra)" menu item send the selected text), the address you enter as a Custom URL, or a dictionary app on your computer (GoldenDict, MDict) or on an Android device (DictTango). The extension's settings stay in your browser's extension storage; the size and position of the dictionary window are kept in the visited site's local storage. The extension has no analytics and no account. Telegram bot — to remember your choices, the bot keeps under your Telegram user ID only the interface language and the city you saved for the Uposatha list (/uposatha reset forgets the city). Our server looks a city name up in the Open-Meteo geocoding service (geocoding-api.open-meteo.com), without your ID. Inline queries are written to the bot's log together with the user ID; the log is kept for 30 days, then deleted. Technical logs — standard request metadata (IP address, User-Agent) is collected by web servers for security purposes and DDoS protection.

Personal identification (except the email address used during Google or Apple Login). Private Telegram chat histories (the bot keeps only what is listed under Telegram bot above). Browsing history outside of our specific services. Persistent tracking identifiers (beyond the scope of a user-initiated sync session).

Our own services: dhamma.gift / dict.dhamma.gift — for search and reader functionality. api.dhamma.gift (and its reserve api2.dhamma.gift) — the DG voices: it receives the text being read aloud, and for the AI search the query text. It also serves the MCP server and the API. files.dhamma.gift — MP3 files of the texts. s.dhamma.gift — other Pali editions side by side. Google Firebase — solely to provide the optional cloud synchronization service, and only if you sign in. External services: dpdict.net — the Digital Pāḷi Dictionary, for dictionary entries our own bundled dictionary does not cover. Only the single Pāḷi word being looked up is sent, with no account, identifier or other context attached. Some of these lookups are made by our server on your behalf; others your browser or the app makes directly, in which case dpdict.net also sees your IP address as it would on any website you visit. This is their service, under their own privacy policy, not ours. sanskrit-lexicon.uni-koeln.de — the Cologne Sanskrit dictionaries. Dict.Dhamma.Gift sends the word being looked up to show Sanskrit entries. Your browser makes the request, so they also see your IP address. Other dictionaries in Dict.Dhamma.Gift — Sutta-Vinaya Definitions and Similes (tripitaka-mcp.com), Gandhari Dictionaries (gandhari.org), PTS Dictionary (dsal.uchicago.edu) and Wisdom Library (wisdomlib.org). Their sections are collapsed by default. When you open one, your browser loads that site's page with the word being looked up. dharmamitra.org — machine translation and grammar explanation. Dhamma.gift, Dict.Dhamma.Gift and the browser extensions link to it (for example "Explain grammar (DharmaMitra)", or DharmaMitra chosen as the dictionary). Only when you use such a link does your browser open DharmaMitra with the selected word or text, so they also see your IP address. Their service, under their own privacy policy. Google Fonts (fonts.googleapis.com, fonts.gstatic.com) — fonts on some pages, such as Settings and Hatthipada. Your browser loads them, so Google sees your IP address. cdnjs.cloudflare.com — a charting script loaded on the Hatthipada page. AI search — only when an exact search finds nothing, or when you press AI mode. The query text is turned into numbers by Cloudflare Workers AI (the bge-m3 model) to find passages by meaning in our own index, and it is sent to a language model from a pool of free services, which names suttas that our index then checks. The pool changes, because we use free tiers: now Google Gemini, Zhipu GLM (Z.ai) and Groq, with DeepSeek and tripitaka-mcp.com in reserve. Our server sends only the query text: your IP address and your account are not passed on. If you want your query to stay on our server, use the exact search: it never leaves it. Google Cloud Text-to-Speech — only when you choose a Google voice: it receives the text being read. On the website your browser sends it to Google directly (with the site's trial key or your own API key), so Google also sees your IP address. In the apps, with the trial key the text goes through our server, which forwards it without identifiers; with your own key the app sends it to Google directly. We do not share, sell, or transmit user data to any third parties for marketing or advertising purposes.

Without synchronization — your history, favorites and settings are not stored on our servers; they remain local to your browser's localStorage. Search queries appear only in the server logs (see below). With synchronization — history, favorites, reading progress, subscriptions, and settings are stored in the Google Cloud database until deleted by the user. Offline library — the full text database (about 260 MB to download, about 680 MB on the device) is downloaded from dhamma.gift and kept on your device only. On the website and in the PWA the download starts only with your consent. The Android and iOS apps always ask before the download, on Wi-Fi too, and name its size; if you say no, the app remembers and does not ask again, and you can still download it in Settings → Offline library. It contains texts only and no data about you. In offline mode, searching and reading texts run on the device without requests to our server. Database updates are offered at most once every two weeks. You can remove the database with the "Delete" button in the offline library settings. Logs — server logs (requests with IP addresses, search queries included) are kept for 14 days, then deleted.

This Privacy Policy may be updated periodically. Your continued use of the Services after such changes constitutes your acceptance of the revised policy. For inquiries regarding your privacy, please contact us at agiftofdhamma@gmail.com. Last updated: November 2026.

Consistency, unified terminology, and attention to the global context make it possible to see the Buddha's teaching with greater depth and subtlety — something impossible with a literary adaptation built on narrowly contextual translation. A precise translation functions as a necessary "bridge," allowing readers to perceive the original structure of the text and the logic of the Dhamma directly, with little or no immersion in linguistics. It fills a missing link for those seeking greater precision and independence in studying primary sources, but who have not yet learned Pali to the required level. This approach does not suggest that all translations should be done this way. Its aim is to fill the empty space between numerous literary adaptations and dense grammatical analyses.

documents.t: Any translation from Pali, or translation of another author's translation — whether a complete text, a text fragment, a dictionary entry, a topical article, or simply a term — in digital, printed, or oral form, as of today () is not considered final but is regarded as "Work in Progress." To obtain a final translation, meanings and terms must be correctly established. If such a translation is possible, it can only be done by an Arahant with the four "analytical knowledges" (catasso paṭisambhidā). Terminology in the Buddha's Teaching must be consistent — this is an integral part of any adequate set of instructions or documents, let alone the Supreme Teacher and Supreme Teaching describing the most subtle, fundamental principles of the universe's workings and the methods of its realization. Dhamma is not fiction. Meanings and definitions are uniform across all texts, especially those concerning the Four Noble Truths and adjacent layers of text. More detail in Rationale. If a concept has a definition in the suttas, that meaning is applied. Example: dukkha has a definition in the suttas — "Pain (dukkha) is bodily pain, bodily discomfort..." (Analysis of Truths, mn141); see also Rationale. A practical example: in the suttas, when dukkha is used in Pali (bodily pain, bodily discomfort), it points the reader to phenomena at the level of rūpa and vedanā. But in translations that lack consistent terminology and render dukkha as "suffering," the reader's attention shifts instead to the level of saññā and saṅkhārā. Ignoring direct term definitions from the suttas is a sub-optimal approach that renders the whole of the Buddha's Teaching not well-formulated (not svākkhāto). If a definition cannot be found in the suttas but can be found in the Vinaya Vibhaṅga (hereinafter Vinaya), that meaning is applied. If a word's definition is found neither in the suttas nor in the Vinaya, a precise systematic translation is preferred over a narrowly contextual one1 — ideally, one word that maximally covers all usage contexts across all or most occurrences in the suttas and Vinaya. More on the issues with narrowly contextual translation in Rationale. If a word occurs too rarely, or only in monotonous cases, and has no definition in the suttas or Vinaya, the global contextual or dictionary meaning is used. If a generally accepted translation or interpretation — including one from a commentary or sub-commentary — contradicts the points above, that translation or interpretation is not applied. If a Pali concept is broader than a single English concept, a word cluster (or a word from that cluster) is used. Example: rāga — fascination-passion; anicca — unreliability, instability, untrustworthiness. Such a cluster may appear at the first occurrence in the text; afterward only the key word is used, as if it had been written: fascination-passion (hereinafter fascination). Or jhāyatha — ignite (ardently strive, concentrate, "meditate," contemplate), hereinafter ignite. If a Pali concept is more specific while the English concept is broader, a clarification is used. Example: ceto — mind-thinking; citta — mind-state; mano — mind-representation, as if it had been written: mind-state (hereinafter mind). Preserving the word order of the Pali sentence is preferred. Preserving Pali grammatical structure is preferred. Consistent, systematic translation of prefixes and endings is preferred, where possible. Preserving the structure of Pali words with negative prefixes is preferred over antonyms. Example: byāpāda and abyāpāda — "hostility" and "non-hostility," not "hostility" and "friendliness." Preserving the structure of compound words as in Pali is preferred. Case endings are used only where the form without them sounds completely unnatural in English. Where possible, it is recommended to omit case endings within compound words,2 preserving their open, polysemantic structure — for example, Noble-Truth is both the truth of the Noble, and a truth leading to nobility, and one from the nobles, and one for becoming noble, and one for those already noble. In cases of semantic divergence, translation should be based on the meaning of the Pali term — as with "false friends of the translator,"3 not by external similarity to English equivalents. More detail in Rationale. Footnotes​ Systematic Translation (Consistent Terminology) is an approach strictly grounded in the direct definitions of terms found within the primary sources (the Suttas and Vinaya). The verified meaning is applied consistently and universally across the entire corpus. Narrowly Contextual (Situational) Translation is the opposite approach: the strict definitions from the Suttas are ignored, and the meaning of a single word changes — sometimes drastically — from text to text, driven by tradition, the translator's taste, or audience expectations. See Rationale for a detailed breakdown. ↩ In addition to the standard understanding of Pali compound words (see e.g. Pali Compounds), it is proposed to take a broader view. As a dash in a date range ("1–10") is not equal only to "1 and 10," a Pali compound such as "ascetics-brahmins" need not mean only "ascetics and brahmins" (although both forms occur in the texts), but the whole spectrum of the spiritual sphere from ascetics to brahmins — as with the whole spectrum from joy to passion in nandīrāga, not only "joy and passion." This approach also allows that, in some cases, splitting a Pali compound for ease of translation can introduce distortions — much like "water runs through a water-pipe" losing something when forced apart into "water" and "pipe" taken separately. A case in point from Pali: Āhārasamudayā kāyassa samudayo — from nourishment-arising, the arising of the body (SN 47.42). The example is subtler than the water-pipe one, but it shows that Pali texts do distinguish between compound words and their "split" counterparts, even though it's commonly assumed there's no such difference. Case endings are used only for words with no suitable compound form in English — so instead of "sufferingo-lamentationo-paino-discontento-despair," it is written "suffering-lamentation-pain-discontent-despair," although the compound reading is implied. ↩ False friends of the translator — words formally similar but with a partial or distorted overlap in meaning. Examples: aggressive — "energetic and also aggressive" vs. "only aggressive, unrelated to energy"; sympathy — "compassion" vs. Russian симпатия — "attraction." ↩
