Dhamma.gift has an MCP server: an AI assistant (Claude, ChatGPT-style clients, Cursor and others) can search the Pali Canon here, read suttas and compare translations on its own, and answer with quotes and links to the reader. It uses the same search engine and the same texts as the site. Address: https://api.dhamma.gift/mcp (Streamable HTTP, no login, read-only). It is listed in the official MCP registry as gift.dhamma/pali-canon. The endpoint is also described in the API docs.

Tool What it does search Keyword, substring or regular-expression search. Returns a list of the matching suttas (id, title, number of matches, reader link): suttas that define the term first, then those named after it, then by how often it occurs. include_segments adds the matched Pali lines, include_translations with langs adds translations. get_text A sutta by id (mn1, dn22, sn56.11): the Pali, and translations when langs is given; editions adds the whole text in the other editions, line by line. compare_editions The canon's editions compared line by line: the Mahāsaṅgīti beside Siam Rath (Thailand), Buddha Jayanti (Sri Lanka), Chaṭṭha Saṅgāyana (Myanmar), the printed Mahāsaṅgīti of 2005 and the PTS editions (DN, MN, SN, AN). A sutta, a line or a range: first a summary per edition, then the lines that differ, word by word. compare_translations One segment (e.g. mn129:21.3) in the Pali, every edition and every available translation side by side. list_structure What exists: collections, books with sutta counts, translation languages and translators; with a prefix (mn, sn56) the list of suttas under it. get_text, compare_editions and compare_translations also return compare_link: the text in the reader's Compare view, every edition beside the translation (e.g. https://dhamma.gift/sn56.11?mode=multi).

Claude (claude.ai / Desktop): Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector → URL https://api.dhamma.gift/mcp. Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http dhamma-gift https://api.dhamma.gift/mcp Other clients: add a remote (HTTP) MCP server with the same URL. Then ask in plain words, for example: "Find all suttas about the turtle, quote the Pali and the Russian translation with links."

The search is literal: it matches letters, not meaning. For a topic the assistant tries the Pali and translation words itself (kacchapa, kummo, turtle, черепаха) and merges the results. At least 3 letters per query; diacritics are ignored (kacchap finds mahākacchapa). Every answer carries reader links: https://dhamma.gift/mn129 for the sutta, https://dhamma.gift/mn129:21.3 for the exact segment. Answers are Pali only unless the assistant asks for translations (include_translations, langs). Sujato's English is left out unless asked for by name; machine (AI) translations are hidden, as in the search on the site. One query lists up to 40 suttas by default; limit takes a number or "all". The answer always gives the true number of matching suttas and says when the list was cut. Regular expressions work as in the site search. Patterns such as kata.*dukkha ("Katamañca … dukkhaṁ?") and vucc.*dukkha ("idaṁ vuccati … dukkhaṁ") find where the canon defines a term.

Our server. core/mcp-server.js in the dg-node repository, mounted as POST /mcp in dg-fastify.js (GET and DELETE answer 405: it is stateless, every request gets its own server object, no sessions). search and get_text are thin wrappers over the functions behind /search and /api/text; compare_translations and list_structure read dg.db directly (read-only). The tool descriptions and a short instruction for the agent (search is literal, try Pali and translation words, quote with the translator and a link) are sent with the server. The plan and open questions (ranking, a stdio mode for the offline app, a separate mcp. subdomain) are in docs/MCP_PLAN.md of the repository.

The site works without a network on top of one artifact: dg.db.gz, a gzipped SQLite database with every text in every language and a trigram FTS index. The same file serves the website (as a PWA) and the Android and iOS apps.

What Path Served as Corpus sources: the Pali texts of six editions (Thai, BJT, Myanmar, Mahāsaṅgīti, its printed MS05, PTS) and the translations siteroot/data/suttacentral.net, siteroot/data/dhammagift (symlinks) — Server database (built) dg.db used by dg-fastify.js: search, reader, API, MCP Offline library siteroot/mobile-data/dg.db.gz /mobile-data/dg.db.gz Its manifest siteroot/mobile-data/db-manifest.json /mobile-data/db-manifest.json Web offline layer public/offline/* (app.js, db-worker.js, core-bundle.js, offline-status.js, offline-library-settings.js, platform.js) /offline/* Shell cache (service worker) public/service-worker.js /sw.js Dictionary (DPD, ~24 MB) public/overrides/js/standalone-dpd/* /assets/js/standalone-dpd/* The artifacts are never committed (hundreds of MB, rebuildable). siteroot/mobile-data/ is a real directory on every host: test and production each have their own.

A copy of the server's dg.db with every language, minus the rows of the translators in OFFLINE_EXCLUDED_TRANSLATORS (ai, bw): those stay on the server, in neither the texts nor the index. The copy is rebuilt from dg.db with the same schema and rowids and its own FTS index, not cut down with DELETE + VACUUM. Its build_id is the hash of its own content. Tables: suttas, texts, html, fts (FTS5, tokenize='trigram remove_diacritics 1', external content over texts), vocab, meta. About 257 MB gzipped and 682 MB on the device. db-manifest.json is what clients read first: { "schema_version": 1, "build_id": "3b0765f32062b0bb", "langs": "all", "fts": "trigram", "source": "dg.db", "built_at": "2026-10-31T12:22:46.130Z", "file_gz": "dg.db.gz", "bytes_gz": 256666299, "bytes": 682291200, "sha256": "…" } sha256 is the hash of the unpacked database. A client never reads build_id from the manifest alone: the downloaded file carries its own meta.build_id, and a file that does not match the build it was saved as is not opened.

The production box does not build the database; the build needs more memory than it has. CI (.github/workflows/build-db.yml) builds dg.db on a GitHub runner and publishes the rolling db-latest release. It carries the server database (dg.db.gz, AI rows included) and the offline library (app-dg.db.gz + app-db-manifest.json), both made by build-search-db.js --publish. The server installs the release with scripts/pull-db.sh. --app also puts the offline library into siteroot/mobile-data/. It checks the unpacked sha256 first, moves the archive into place, and writes the manifest last, so a reader never sees a manifest for a file that is not there yet. On a machine with enough memory the same steps run locally: npm run build-search-db # siteroot/data/* -> dg.db (the full corpus, FTS5 trigram) npm run publish-offline-db # build-search-db.js --publish: dg.db.gz + db-manifest.json into siteroot/mobile-data/ node build-search-db.js --publish --no-build # publish the dg.db already there, without building again --out=<dir> publishes into another directory. A new build_id in the manifest is what tells every reader who already has the library that an update is available, so publishing is always a deliberate step.
documents.s: How it is built and published

documents.t: distBase = window.DG_DIST_BASE || '/mobile-data' (public/offline/platform.js). Fetch db-manifest.json. The room needed (the database plus its archive) is checked before any download starts. A private (incognito) window is refused with a plain message: the storage probe fails there, or the quota is under ~300 MB. A normal window short of space is told how much is needed and how much is free. Download dg.db.gz into a scratch file at the OPFS root (dg-mobile.<build_id>.gz.partial). An interrupted download continues with an HTTP Range request from the byte it stopped at (a later visit too), and a cancel deletes the scratch file. Unpack the complete archive from disk with DecompressionStream into the SQLite pool (opfs-sahpool, named dg-offline) as /dg-mobile.<build_id>.db. The unpacked size must match bytes. Verify: a cheap check gates the install (rows readable). The full PRAGMA quick_check runs in the background and can still invalidate the library. A worker (@sqlite.org/sqlite-wasm) answers /search, /api/text/:id, /api/nav/:id; the site's own fetch is shimmed before any other script runs. It runs the same core/search-core.js as the server (core-bundle.js). Updates: the page compares the open library's build_id with the manifest's and offers the new one. The new build downloads beside the old one, which keeps answering until the new file is proven; then the old file is removed. The shell (HTML, JS, CSS, wasm, core-bundle.js) is cached by the service worker. The dictionary is cached by the page right after the library is adopted, because the service worker's install pass alone proved unreliable (see below). Without the library, a text read once still opens again offline: the service worker keeps the latest 200 texts read (/api/text/…). Only one tab owns the OPFS pool (a single-writer resource). The tab in front takes it over, and a tab without it can be served by the owner over a BroadcastChannel.

The apps fetch the same dg.db.gz with their own native downloaders, so a download survives the app going to the background or the screen locking: Android: DgDownloadService, a foreground service with progress in a notification. The worker then imports the file from the app's storage, the same way as above. iOS: DgDownloadPlugin.swift (a background URLSession). The library is kept as a plain dg.db in the App Group container and read with native SQLite (DgSharedLibrary.swift), because the Share Extension, a separate process, searches the same file. The worker sends its queries there instead of to OPFS.

npm run test-offline # end-to-end: install, offline search/reader/TOC, parity against dg.db and dg-fastify npm run test-offline-parity # the worker's core bundle vs core/search-core.js npm run test-offline-resume # truncated response -> Range resume npm run test-offline-outage # a real outage: pm2 dg-test stopped, nginx answering 503; search, language, a second tab, TOC, reader test-offline-outage always restores the service. DevTools "offline" only makes requests reject; a stopped server also answers 5xx, which is the case that used to break the shell. The pm2 processes are dg-test and dg-prod.

OPFS requires a secure context (HTTPS or localhost). The browser may evict storage; the page asks for persistent storage, and a missing library is a normal state the UI reports ("Settings → Offline library"). A 5xx must fall back to the cache, and a cache miss must rethrow. respondWith(undefined) is a TypeError in the page ("Failed to convert value to 'Response'") and a spinner that never stops. The service worker's install-time precache can silently miss entries (127 of ~145 in one measured run, with the server answering those files 200). Anything that must be there offline is cached from the page as well. The server answers Vary: Origin (CORS), and a page's fetch() carries an Origin the precache's own requests did not, so the service worker looks its cache up with ignoreVary (same-origin GETs only); without it every fetch()ed file missed offline. Tab lifecycle: a page in the back/forward cache keeps its worker and the pool handles. So the worker is terminated on pagehide (never during a download), and the library is re-opened on focus/visibilitychange/pageshow.

The Dhamma.Gift voice is a text-to-speech service: the same one that reads in the site's player and the dictionary. It can be called from a browser or a server, no key, no login. Terms of use pratham, priyamvada, alan, kathleen, irina, puriso may be used freely, within the limits below and each voice's own licence. dg, dgru, dgen (Cūḷa DG, Yojanāni DG) are made from recordings of real people's voices. All rights reserved. They may be used only on the Dhamma.Gift website and in the Dhamma.Gift apps. Any other use through this API — personal and non-commercial included — requires prior written permission from Dhamma.Gift. Address: https://api.dhamma.gift · CORS is open · a limit of 60 requests per minute per IP.

POST /api/tts/pali with JSON: Field Meaning text the text, up to 2000 characters. Pāḷi in IAST (Evaṁ me sutaṁ), a translation in English or Russian voice the voice (below); pratham by default rate speed, 0.25–3; 1 is the voice's own pace (the site reads Pāḷi at 0.875) The answer is {"audioContent": "<base64 MP3>"} — the same shape as Google's Text-to-Speech, so a player written for Google plays it as is. MP3, mono, 22 kHz, ~40 kbit/s; repeated requests come from a cache. curl -s https://api.dhamma.gift/api/tts/pali -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"text":"Evaṁ me sutaṁ.","voice":"pratham","rate":0.875}' \ | python3 -c 'import json,sys,base64; open("evam.mp3","wb").write(base64.b64decode(json.load(sys.stdin)["audioContent"]))' const r = await fetch('https://api.dhamma.gift/api/tts/pali', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ text: 'Evaṁ me sutaṁ.', voice: 'pratham', rate: 0.875 }) }); new Audio('data:audio/mp3;base64,' + (await r.json()).audioContent).play();

voice Language What it is pratham Pāḷi "Pratham": Piper neural voice + our Pāḷi pronunciation rules (IAST → sounds, stress, long vowels). Default dg Pāḷi "Cūḷa DG": a voice trained on real Pāḷi readings. Beta priyamvada Pāḷi "Priyamvada": a female Piper voice with the same rules dgen, alan, kathleen English Piper voices. dgen is "Yojanāni DG" (the default): trained on a real person's readings. Pāḷi words and abbreviations (Ven., SN 56.11) are read properly puriso, dgru, irina Russian Piper voices. dgru is "Cūḷa DG" (the default); puriso is Supertonic's male voice M1 taught to Piper. Pāḷi in Latin script is read the Pāḷi way, Russian words with the right stress GET /api/tts/dg-voices gives the list as {"voices": [{"id", "lang", "label"}]} in menu order (a language's first voice is its default; Yojanāni DG is listed there by its internal id miles, which works the same as dgen); GET /api/tts/health shows that the service is up and which version of the pronunciation rules it uses. GET /api/tts/offline/pali-ipa.json gives the rules, the engine and the voice models that DG downloads to read on the device, offline. How Pāḷi is read: every letter is sounded, punctuation becomes pauses, …pe… is read as "peyyāla".

POST /api/tts/memo — the lines read one after another with pauses of any length between them (Google stops at 10 seconds); this is what the Memo page saves. Field Meaning segments the lines, up to 200 and 20 000 characters in all voice, rate as above delay the pause between lines, seconds, up to 3600 end_delay the pause at the end, seconds, up to 3600 sound gong.mp3 or tick.mp3 at the end, or empty The answer is the MP3 itself (audio/mpeg): the speech itself at most 30 minutes, the whole file with its pauses at most 180. One such request counts as ten against the per-minute limit.

It's the same bot under two names — @Dhammagift_bot and its short form @Dgift_bot — same functionality, either one works. It works in two ways: inline, right in the message box of any chat or group, and in its own chat, where the same things work plus the commands and the settings.

Type @dgift_bot in the message box of any chat and then a Pali word (kacchapa), a text number (mn10, sn56.11) or Velthuis transliteration (.t .d .n ~n aa ii uu → ṭ ḍ ṇ ñ ā ī ū, so satipa.t.thaana works as well as satipaṭṭhāna). Telegram answers with: ✏️ Send: <text> — the main result: that text with links to the site and the dictionary; dictionary words that match what you typed — pick one, and the message uses the proper spelling with diacritics. In the frame: what is typed in the message box of any chat or group, not in the bot's own chat. If the word is in the built-in mini dictionary (the Pāli–English one, with a Russian translation for the Russian interface), its short meaning is shown in the list under the word, and in the sent message — between the word and the links: kacchapa — masc. tortoise; turtle; lit. drinking marsh A form is traced back to its dictionary word (kacchapā → kacchapa), up to four words are shown with … if there are more (the list is not exhaustive), the part of speech is in italics, and when there is no Russian translation of a word the English one is shown. Machine-translated Russian entries are marked [пер. ИИ]. Above the list there is a button — 🔎 Open Dhamma.gift En: sn56.11 — it opens Dhamma.gift as a Mini App with the query already searched.

A picked result lands in the chat as a message of the bot: the text, the links and, under the message, the buttons. 🔎 Dhamma.gift in the message and the Read at 🔎 Dhamma.gift En button lead to the same place: a text number (sn56.11) opens the text itself in the reader, a word opens the site's search; 📘 Dictionary — the word in the dictionaries (dict.dhamma.gift); its short meaning from the mini dictionary is already in the message, above the links. An extra word does not break the link: mn10 metta still opens mn10. The same search and reader are the Mini Apps behind /extra: search, reading, dictionary and Memo.

/uposatha in the bot's chat, or @dgift_bot uposatha in any chat — the next 30 days as the suttas count them: the 8th, 14th and 15th lunar day of each half-month, six days a month. Without a city the list is the one for Bodh Gaya, with Bodh Gaya's real sunset, dawn and noon times. @dgift_bot uposatha Chiang Mai (or /uposatha Chiang Mai) — the same days with the real sun times of a city: when the day begins (sunset), dawn, noon and when it ends (the next sunset). /uposatha <city> in the bot's chat also remembers the city, so the bare command keeps using it; /uposatha reset forgets it. The inline query does not remember the city. An empty inline query — @dgift_bot and a space — shows the Uposatha list for your saved city, or for Bodh Gaya if there is none. In the frame: what is typed in the message box of any chat or group, not in the bot's own chat. The dates are the same for everybody — the moon is one — and only the sun times are local. The list ends with Times: begin · dawn · noon · end, and two buttons sit under the message: the Ru/En switch and the link to the full calendar at dhamma.gift/uposatha-calendar. How to read these days is on the Uposatha days page. The same calendar is an app with widgets, Uposatha by the Suttas: App Store · Google Play · Microsoft Store.

Search and reading work here too — just without @dgift_bot: send a word (saariputta) or a text number (mn10), and you get the same message with the same links and buttons. For the Uposatha days use /uposatha: a plain uposatha is searched as a word. On top of that, the bot has commands and settings. Command What it does /start the welcome message, with a button that switches the interface language /language choose the interface language (English / Русский) /extra links to the Mini Apps: search, reading, dictionary, and the 🛞 Memo button (in the bot's own chat) /docs the link to this documentation /uposatha Uposatha days for the next 30 days

Language — /language (two buttons, the current one is checked) sets it; the Русский / English button under the /start welcome message and the Lang En/Ru / Язык Ru/En button under a search message switch it. The choice is remembered and affects the links: the Russian interface leads to dhamma.gift/<query>?lang=ru and dict.dhamma.gift/ru/<query>. The city for the Uposatha list — /uposatha <city> remembers it, /uposatha reset forgets it, and the empty /uposatha keeps showing it. The Menu button next to the message box (DG en / DG ru) — opens dhamma.gift as a Mini App in the language you chose.

A canon-wide table of contents (Sutta Piṭaka + Vinaya), separate from the reader's own per-sutta TOC (see Reader) — this one lets you browse the whole collection and jump straight into a chapter. You can also open it from anywhere on the site — Alt+2. Open in a new window

Lazy tree — books and chapters expand on demand instead of loading the whole canon up front. Translator filter — a side panel with a "Find a translator…" search box, a separate group of checkboxes per language (with a text count next to each translator), and a select-all checkbox per group. Less-common translators are tucked behind a "More" link. Filtering hides entire books/chapters that have nothing matching, rather than just greying out individual rows. Collapsible side panel — open/closed state is remembered (localStorage), open by default on wide screens and closed by default on phones. Inline Pātimokkha preview — the bhikkhu/bhikkhunī Pātimokkha sections expand right on the page, with Pali text and a built-in audio player for each sub-section, no need to jump into the full reader: In the Pātimokkha list, a rule's title opens the rule; the Story link next to it opens the rule's analysis in the Vibhaṅga. The Show the Pātimokkha switch in the filter panel shows or hides both Pātimokkhas. Short URLs — /toc/<id> opens the TOC scrolled straight to a given section (e.g. /toc/mn, /toc/sn25). The translator filter is a saved setting Once you uncheck something, it stays unchecked on your next visit — easy to forget, and then wonder why some translations seem to have "disappeared". While the filter is active, a "Filter active — reset" link appears at the top of the filter panel.

The * next to "Khuddaka Nikāya" means not every book in the collection is shown — by default just Itivuttaka, Udāna, Suttanipāta, Dhammapada, Theragāthā and Therīgāthā. Hover the asterisk to see the list: The remaining books (Jātaka and others) turn on from the Quick Settings panel → "Where to search" — see Search — the same toggle also controls what's visible here, in the TOC.

documents.t: Work in progress. A CAT (Computer-Assisted Translation) editor for line-by-line translation of Pali Canon texts — convenient input, quick templates, and two ways to work with the text. Open in a new window Demo This is a demo with SN 56.11 and an existing translation loaded; saving does not work here. The editor opens for everyone: the Pali text and the published translations. Saving to the server, and loading the AI draft translations into the Russian editor, are for translators: sign in with Google (the sign-in icon at the end of the top bar; without it, Save still downloads the file and says “Sign in with Google first.”).

◀ ▶ — previous/next text. Sutta number — type an id (e.g. sn56.11, an3.70), with auto-detection of whether a translation already exists. Source language — pick the source file's language. DT.org — open dhammatalks.org/suttas/. DG — open the current text on Dhamma.Gift. Update — reload the translation from source. Find/Replace — a search-and-replace window (escape (, ), [, ] as \(, \), \[, \]). Format (checkbox) — auto-format line breaks. Clear — clear the input field. Open file / Load from server — open a previously saved draft. Save — download the translation as JSON and, for a signed-in translator, save it on the server. In the top bar: ? opens the instructions, with a video tutorial; ru switches to the Russian editor; the Diff Checker icon opens an external tool for comparing text versions.

A two-column table (Text | Translation) — each row is edited separately. Click a cell — edit it. The 🔗 icon — jump to this row in quick-entry mode. ↑ / ← at the start of a cell — move to the cell above. ↓ / → at the end of a cell — move to the cell below. Enter — add an empty row, or wrap text onto a new row. Ctrl+Enter — move text to the start of the next row. Backspace at the start of a row — merge with the previous row. Delete at the end of a row — merge with the next row.

One large text field — the whole translation at once, synced live with the table. Ctrl+Q (or the button after Find/Replace) — select a range of rows and merge them into one. Ctrl+Shift+F / Ctrl+Shift+H — open Find/Replace (same escaping for ()/[]).

Inside the Find/Replace window there are buttons for phrases that come up over and over in the canon. One click inserts the text at the cursor (in this editor, the inserted text is in Russian): 4nt / 4nt short (the Four Noble Truths formula, full and short), n8p / n8p short (the Noble Eightfold Path), Thus said… (a sutta's closing formula), plus an em-dash, curly quotes, and an inverted question mark for punctuation.
Save names the file by the text and the translator (sn56.11_translation-en-thanissaro.json); the tr. o checkbox next to Format puts o in place of the translator — for final versions.

"There are these five dangers, monks, for one who recites the Dhamma in a drawn-out singing voice." — AN 5.209 Try it: the line below is already selected — press ▶ at the bottom of the frame and listen: Open in a new window

Click the 🔉 icon next to the text's title: next to the Pali title it reads the Pali, next to a translation's title that translation. Click any Pali or translation sentence to highlight it, then press the ▶ button that appears at the bottom. Tap the ✦ before or after a line and choose Voice in its menu. Open a link to a line (for example /an5.209:1.1): the line is highlighted and ▶ is already there. Press Alt+R (Option+R on Mac). On the search results page Alt+R reads the quotes found, in the same player: each sutta's name first, then its quotes, and the row being read is highlighted.

Controls — Play/Pause, previous/next sentence. Navigation — pause, click a Pali sentence to highlight it, press Play to resume from there. Mode — what is read: Pāḷi / Pāḷi + translation / translation / translation + Pāḷi. Speed — the speed button opens a slider with presets; the default for Pāḷi is 0.7× ("normal" for the DG voice). Memo — opens the Memo page. AB — the A-B loop. Settings (⚙) — Scroll (S: the text follows the voice), the pause between phrases in seconds, Pause only between paragraphs, and Voice settings.

⚙ → Voice settings has two rows, Pāḷi and Translation: tap a row, pick the kind (DG Voice, Google Cloud or System), then the voice; for Google, first its language. The ▶ next to a row plays a short sample (DG voices). ↺ brings back the default voices; downloaded voices stay. On the first play a tip lists the three kinds; × hides it. The first neural voices that speak Pāḷi DG Voice are the first neural voices that read Pāḷi as plain speech, not chant: with Pāḷi's long and short vowels, and without the singing voice AN 5.209 warns about.

They run on our server: no key, no limits, nothing to install. Each one can also be downloaded to your device and then reads without internet. Pāḷi Pratham ♂ · Piper (default): reads Pāḷi by our pronunciation rules. Cūḷa DG ♂ · beta: trained on real Pāḷi readings. Priyamvada ♀ · Piper: a female voice, the same pronunciation rules. English: Yojanāni DG ♂ (US, default), Alan ♂ (UK), Kathleen ♀ (US). Russian: Cūḷa DG ♂ (default), Puriso ♂, Irina ♀. Pāḷi words inside a translation (sutta, Dhamma, bhikkhu, names) are read the Pāḷi way. Abbreviations are spelled out (Ven. → Venerable, SN 56.11 → Saṁyutta Nikāya 56, 11). Russian words get their stress from the context (дела́ его / иметь де́ла), online and with a downloaded voice alike, and ё where the text prints е. The next sentences are prepared while one is playing, so there are no gaps between them.
documents.s: DG Voice — our own free neural voices (default)

documents.t: Pāḷi: rare words and long compounds are sometimes pronounced inaccurately. Pāḷi: a line of one or two words sounds less clear than the same words inside a phrase. Cūḷa DG (Pāḷi): the sound is still rougher than Pratham's. Russian: where the stress depends on the meaning (за́мок / замо́к), it is sometimes wrong. Kathleen: low sound quality.

In Voice settings → DG Voice, each voice in the list has a ⬇ icon with its download size. Once downloaded, the voice reads on your device with no network, on the reader and on the Memo page. The 🗑 icon deletes it. The English and Russian voices download a shared pronunciation module with the first of them. While a DG voice is reading online, the player itself offers Listen offline · Download with the voice's size; × hides the offer. Cūḷa DG and Yojanāni DG voices: all rights reserved The Cūḷa DG and Yojanāni DG voices are made from recordings of real people's voices. All rights in these voices and their models are reserved. Permitted only: downloading these voices and listening to texts with them on the Dhamma.Gift website and in the Dhamma.Gift apps. Prohibited without prior written permission from Dhamma.Gift: any use of these voices or their models outside the Dhamma.Gift website and apps, personal and non-commercial use included; copying, distributing, publishing or passing on the model files to third parties; cloning or imitating these voices; training or fine-tuning other models on these models or on the audio they produce; any commercial use. This restriction is also stated in the file of each such model.

High-quality cloud voices. Pāḷi is read by a Punjabi (pa-IN) voice through Devanagari with our own fixes. They work with a built-in trial key; for regular use enter your own Google API key (see below), whose free monthly quota is generous for personal use.
documents.s: Google — cloud voices with a free quota

documents.t: Uses the speech synthesis of your system or browser: no internet needed, nothing is sent anywhere. There is no Pāḷi voice in any system, so install one of Sanskrit (India), Hindi (India), Nepali or Indonesian for the closest pronunciation; if none is installed, English is used as a fallback. Android — Settings → Accessibility → Text-to-speech output, then install voice data for the language: Android help. iPhone / iPad — Settings → Accessibility → Spoken Content → Voices: Apple help. Mac — System Settings → Accessibility → Spoken Content → System voice → Manage Voices: Apple help. Windows — Settings → Time & language → Speech → Manage voices → Add voices: Microsoft help. After installing a voice, reload the page and pick it in Voice settings → System.
documents.s: System — your device's voices, work offline

documents.t: The AB button next to the player is a separate tool layered on top of normal playback: pick a start and end point in the text, and the player repeats just that passage, with a pause between repeats and a repeat limit (or infinite). Click AB — if a line was already selected, it immediately becomes point A and the panel waits for you to click a line for point B; if nothing was selected, click a line for A first, then for B. As soon as both points are set, the loop starts automatically. The panel opens under the player; AB opens and closes it again. Pause between loops — seconds to wait between repeats (− / + or type a number). Repeats — defaults to ∞ (infinite); set your own number and the loop stops on its own once it's done. The 🗑 button clears both points. To move a point, click it again and pick a new line. To clear a point, right-click (or long-press on phones) directly on the A or B button. The passage between the two points is marked in the text with a vertical bar on the left.
documents.s: A-B loop — repeat a passage for memorization

documents.t: Key Action Alt+R Toggle Voice Mode S Toggle autoscroll Space Play / Pause ← → or ↑ ↓ Previous / Next segment 1 Mode: Pāḷi 2 Mode: Pāḷi + Translation 3 Mode: Translation 4 Mode: Translation + Pāḷi + / - Increase / decrease speed R Reset speed to default Space and the arrow keys only work with auto-scroll on If "Autoscroll" is off (the S key, or the toggle in the player settings), Space and the arrow keys stop responding to player control — that's expected behavior, not a bug. The 1–4 keys and +/- always work, regardless of autoscroll.
Voice settings — kinds of voices, languages and voices, samples, the Google API key. File — a link to an audio file, when one exists for that text. Help ? — this page.

Only for the Google voices, when the trial key isn't enough. Create a project in Google Cloud, enable the Text-to-Speech API and create an API key (how to start); once a Google voice is chosen, Voice settings shows a key field under the two rows: paste it there. Free monthly limits and prices: Google Cloud pricing. By default translations use the cheaper Standard voices, Pāḷi a premium one.

For some texts, an MP3: line under the text (for example MP3: Pali · English) gives the whole sutta as one file, in Pāḷi and in the translation, read by the DG voices; hover the translation link to see the translator. The Vinaya's two Vibhaṅgas have audio as well: Pāḷi for 347 rules and Russian for 34.
On the Memo page the ⬇ button saves the text as one MP3 in the voice you chose: with the DG voice the pauses between lines can be of any length (Google's are limited to 10 seconds).

The Uposatha is a special day for intensified practice — the 14th, 15th and 8th lunar day of each half-month. A list of the key suttas, from which you can work out for yourself when and how to keep the Uposatha, is here. The calendar shows the Uposatha days as the suttas describe them. Below is the real page, a live demo. Open in a new window

iPhone and iPad — Uposatha by the Suttas on the App Store: the calendar as an app, with reminders and widgets for the home screen and the lock screen. Android — Uposatha by the Suttas on Google Play: the calendar as an app, with reminders and home-screen widgets; a long press on its icon shows the next Uposatha days. Windows 11 — Uposatha by the Suttas in the Microsoft Store: the calendar in its own window and three widgets for the Widgets Board (Win + W, then "+"). Uposatha + kala — how long to the next Uposatha day and whether it is the time for food now; Day & night — the part of the day or night that is going on; Month — the month with the Uposatha days marked. Telegram — /uposatha in the chat of @dgift_bot, or @dgift_bot uposatha Chiang Mai typed in any chat: the next 30 days with the sun times of your city. More on the Telegram bot page. Any browser — the calendar page; the browser's menu installs it as a web app (the "Web App" badge at the bottom of the page does the same where the browser allows it).

Five tabs (at the top on a wide screen, at the bottom on a phone). Summary gives the Moon now — its phase, the lit part and the lunar day — with a countdown to the next Uposatha, the Meals card and "From the suttas", passages on the Uposatha ("Show all" lists them). Uposathas has two views: "By dates", a table with the beginning and the end of each Uposatha and the Moon, and "Uposatha days", a list by months and weeks. Calendar is an ordinary month with the days marked; tap a date for its details. Night–day is the structure of the night and day (below), and Suttas the key suttas, each opening at the passage. Dates. A day in the suttas begins in the evening ("night and day", AN 3.70), so an Uposatha is dated by the evening it begins and lasts through the night and the next day. In the month calendar the evening date has a ring; the next date, the day of that Uposatha, has a dashed ring. When the 14th and the 15th follow each other, the three dates read 14 · 14–15 · 15: on the middle one the 14th is still going in the day and the 15th begins in the evening. The 15th is filled; the 8th and the 14th are rings. The lines of a date. Begins — the evening; Ends — the next evening; Lunar day — the real lunar day of that Uposatha, for checking (with "Details" on, also its age and when it ends). Real lunar days are numbered 1 to 30 through the month (the Moon gains 12° on the Sun each day); the suttas name the days by their number within a half, so the 8th day of the waning half is the 23rd of the month and the 14th of the waning half the 29th. A lunar day changes at an exact moment, not at midnight, and lasts 19 to 26 hours, so against the calendar dates a number sometimes appears twice or is skipped; the calendar reads this from the real Moon and says so in a note under the date. The lunar day is read at the dawn that follows the evening, because the daytime of the Uposatha lies there. The full and the new moon are moments and often fall on the next date; they are marked on the date they really fall on, with the time. Dates can differ by a day. The moments come from an astronomical model, accurate to about a minute. Thai, Sri Lankan and Burmese communities calculate their calendars by tradition and can differ from these dates by a day; if you keep the Uposatha with a particular community, follow its calendar.

Open the settings (the gear ⚙ at the top). They are in folding groups — "General settings" (language, theme, font size), "Uposatha settings", "Meals", "Parts of the night and day" and "Test reminders"; what you leave open is remembered. The link "change" on the Summary tab and "set a place" on the Night–day tab lead straight to the place. Time zone and hemisphere (under "Advanced"). The moments are shown in your time zone; the hemisphere decides which side of the Moon is lit in the pictures. When a place is set, both are taken from it and the manual fields are hidden. Place. With your location (or a city typed in the field) the evening is the real sunset and the sun's times are shown; without it the evening is taken at 18:00 and the day parts at 06:00 – 18:00, marked with an asterisk. The location is used only in your browser, rounded to about a kilometre, and is not sent anywhere. "Update my place automatically on opening" finds it again once a day, so the times follow you when you travel. Week starts on. Monday or Sunday; until you choose, Monday in Russian and Sunday in English. By the suttas. On — the Uposatha as in the suttas, six days a month, counted from the evening. Off — the modern scheme: four days a month, the dates of the new moon, the first quarter, the full moon and the last quarter (the label turns burgundy so that it is not mistaken). Details. Off — every date in one short line. Moon of every day in the calendar. On — the Calendar tab draws the Moon in every date, not only on the Uposatha days. Twilight. "Dawn and dusk" lets you count the day from sunrise and sunset, or from civil, nautical or astronomical twilight. It needs a place. Reminders. "Remind in advance" — choose when, from "when it begins" up to two days before; "Remind on the Uposatha day" — at the time you set (06:00 by default). Then the sound and the days: by default the 8th and the 14th; the 15th can be added. The reminder for the 14th says that there are two Uposatha days, the 14th and the 15th. On the site a reminder comes only while the page is open or running in the background of your device (the sound you choose plays then too); Safari and iPhone can hold it back. In the apps for Android and iPhone the reminders are set on the device itself and arrive with the app closed, each with its own sound. Or add the days to your phone's calendar. Your own calendar (on the site; in the apps the reminders are the device's own). The button "Add to calendar" (and the same row in the settings) opens the options: Apple opens the subscription in Apple Calendar (also other apps that accept a webcal link); Google opens the "add by URL" form in Google Calendar; Copy link gives the link for any other program. A subscription (the /uposatha.ics feed) covers the coming year and renews itself. Nothing is stored on our side — the link carries your choices (place, scheme, reminder time), so the same link gives the same calendar to whoever opens it. Apple Calendar keeps the alarms from the feed; Google Calendar ignores them for subscribed calendars and uses its own default notifications. Download .ics file adds the next 12 months once, with alarms, to any calendar. It does not update afterwards. Share copies the link to the page or opens the share sheet of your device.

The card "Meals" shows the time for food (dawn to midday) or vikāla, "the wrong time" (midday to the next dawn; Pc 37). Midday is counted by the sun, the middle of the day, or the clock. The bell in the corner of the card switches on reminders for the end (default sound: the Vinaya definition of vikāla, read aloud) and for the beginning of the time for food; in the settings they can come on Uposatha days or every day.

The suttas divide the day into three parts — pubbaṇhasamaya (morning), majjhanhikasamaya (midday) and sāyanhasamaya (evening) — and the night into three parts — paṭhama yāma, majjhima yāma and pacchima yāma (MN 53; AN 8.9; Ud 1.1). The page cuts the time from sunrise to sunset into three equal parts, and from sunset to sunrise likewise, for your place and today's date, and marks the part that is going on now. This is conventional, for illustration: the suttas give no clock times, and the parts are longer or shorter with the season. What is written by each part — alms in the morning, seclusion at midday, meeting in the evening; walking and sitting, the lion's posture, rising — is how the arahants and other monks of the suttas spend it (SN 28.1, MN 53): a picture from the suttas, not a rule; a layperson is not required to do so. The word majjhanhikasamaya itself is in MN 79 ("the sun at midday"); SN 28.1 does not use it, but describes that part of the day: after the meal, the day's meditation, coming out in the evening. Reminders of the parts. The "Remind" bell by the "Day" heading sets a reminder at the start of each part: by default only the day parts, on Uposatha days, with the part's name read aloud in Pali. The night parts, every day and the sound are in the menu.
